body: Rathnapura Maha Saman Dewalaya, located in the heart of Sri Lanka's gem city, is a significant spiritual and cultural landmark. Dedicated to Saman, the patron deity of Sabaragamuwa, this temple offers visitors a serene and deeply spiritual atmosphere. The architecture is a blend of traditional Sri Lankan styles with intricate carvings and vibrant murals. The temple is renowned for its annual festival, which attracts thousands of pilgrims. The surrounding lush greenery and peaceful environment enhance its charm. Whether you're seeking spiritual solace or cultural insight, Rathnapura Maha Saman Dewalaya provides a profound experience for all visitors.

body: It was a religious visit for us. However, the . paintings and architecture would be totally worth seeing. You could be a part of the experience by lighting by following the common traditions too. Flowers, oil lamps and incense sticks could be bought from the small shops beside the road that you enter the temple (or "devaalaya") premises. Oil lamps and incense could lit in the ground level and then you could climb up the stairs all the way to the temple (if you're lucky you'll be there to witness the pooja as well). It will be a little crowded inside if during the time of the pooja but its not unbearable. Do not miss the stupa and the shrine room on either side of the temple. You can offer flowers to either of these places. Word has it that you can wish for good deeds that you want to come true and if they do come true, you could pay a return to pay your respects. :)
title: Paintings and architecture worth seeing

body: A shrine dedicated to deity Saman who is the guardian god to Sabaragamuwa province. The ancient chronicals reveals that he was the leader of the Deva tribe in ancient Lanka and one of the great follower of Lord Buddha. The Lord Saman is greatly venerated by Sabaragamuwa peaople in other words people in Ratnapura district. September is the festive month for the Devale. There is a annual procession also. Although the history of the Saman devale runs to the Anuradhapura era. Present shrine had built in Dambadeniya era by a minister called Aryakamadeva. During Portuguese era it was captured and destroyed. They used the premises as a fortress. King Seethawaka Rajasinghe recaptured it and renovated. You can easily reach there bu A4 highway. When you travel from Colombo, close to Ratnapura town turn your right to Panadura Ratnapura road at Moragahayata junction and proceed 1.5km ahead. The entrance is free. Parking available. It is heavily crowded during festival season in August and September.
title: Sacred place dedicated to Lord Saman
